newsitem.title: UK: Labour promises British drinkers a full pint.
newsitem.headline: Labour promises British drinkers a full pint.

text.p: Britain's opposition Labour Party promised on Tuesday to give beer drinkers a full pint by making oversized glasses with a line to mark the pint mandatory.
"Customers who order and pay for a pint of beer are entitled to get a full pint," Labour industry spokesman Nigel Griffiths told reporters.

Recent survey evidence shows that drinkers are getting short changed, he said. The Campaign for Real Ale (CAMRA), a consumer group which champions traditional British beer, published a national survey at the same time which revealed eight out of ten pints are sold short.
"Lined beer glasses will ensure that every beer drinker gets the full pint he or she has paid for. I reject claims that this legislation could force up the price of a pint," said Griffiths.

The Labour Party, clear favourites to win an election likely to be held on May 1, will reinstate section 43 of the Weights and Measures Act 1985 and insist that publicans replace their glass stock, as it gets broken, with new oversized, lined glasses within a year.

This would clear up confusion about where the law stands on short measure pints after recent court cases rejected guidance notes from the Brewers Licensed Retailers Association (BLRA), Griffiths said.

The ruling Conservative Party decided not to legislate for a full pint in 1993 saying that any move to introduce oversized glasses would force the price of a pint to the drinker up by about seven pence.

"It will mean extra cost and burden on the industry which will add about eight pence to a pint," said Tim Hampson of the Brewers and Licensed Retailers Association, whose members include Britain's three main brewers Whitbread Plc, Scottish and Newcastle Plc and Bass Plc
He argued the increase would reflect the cost of changing over glasses as well as providing the extra beer and metric, automated dispensers in place of traditional hand-pulled pumps.
"That does not mean we support a short measure," said Hamson.
Griffiths said the changeover from traditional glasses to oversized ones would cost nothing if the new glasses were phased in over 12 months, the average lifetime of a traditional pint glass.
Bringing in oversized glasses would also remove the current problem of spillage, he said.
Despite hostility from the BLRA, pubs company J.D. Wetherspoon Plc and Wolverhampton & Dudley Breweries Plc support a change to the law.
